concepts.def: Hierarchical division of society into ranked groups based on power, wealth and status.
Davis and Moore (1945): inequality is necessary to motivate the most talented into the most important roles.
Society polarised into bourgeoisie (own means of production) and proletariat (sell labour); class conflict drives history.
Stratification involves class (economic), status (prestige) and party (power); more nuanced than Marx.
Weber's term for opportunities to gain valued resources (health, education, income) shaped by social position.
Measure of income inequality from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (one person has all); UK around 0.36 (ONS).

walkthroughs.body_html:
Social Inequality — a core area of GCSE Sociology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Social Inequality brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Social Inequality.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

options: Unnecessary
Necessary to motivate talent
A capitalist conspiracy
Disappearing

Party

mcqs.q: Why do postmodernists reject Murdock's universal nuclear family thesis?
options: A self-fulfilling prophecy is when teachers predict the future accurately.
Because Marx proved families are exploitative.
Because nuclear families no longer exist at all.
Family forms are now diverse and fluid - no single type dominates.
